title: Living ashtpadi 5

lines: YEARS PASS; IT FEELS LIKE MINE.
cards: A moneylender, a saahu, hands a trader capital to work with. The trader buys, sells, eats well, throws a wedding. Years pass, and he starts to think of the money as his own.
Then one day the saahu asks for some of it back. Not all. Some.

And the trader is furious, as though he's being robbed. Anyone watching can see what's happened, anyone except the trader. The second stanza of ashtpadi five tells a story like that, and it shows what gratitude is for.

teach.h: THE BANKER LENDS; THE MAN FEASTS.
teach.b: Guru Arjan tells it plainly. The banker gives his capital. The man eats and drinks and lives in delight.
Then the banker takes back a little of what was only ever held in trust, and the ignorant one rages. By his anger he loses his own credit; nobody will trust him with anything again.

teach.h: PUT IT BACK BEFORE THE OWNER.
teach.b: Then the turn: the wise one places what belongs to the owner back before the owner, and accepts the order with his forehead bowed. That person, the stanza says, is made happy four times over.
Put that next to the last three days. The salok named God the Giver. The ten things showed how gifts slip behind our backs.
The empty table asked what anyone could say if they were all gone. Now the banker shows the long game. Gratitude isn't only a nice feeling.
It's how you stay trustworthy with what you've been lent. The trader who forgot it was a loan couldn't let any of it go. And everything goes, in the end: health, strength, time, people you love.
What it offers is a way of holding it all now, as a trust, so that when some is called back, the hands are already open.
That's why gratitude is this ashtpadi's practice: not a mood, but a habit of counting, so the ten never fall behind the back.

how: Sikhs speak of all they have as Waheguru's gift held in trust, and gratitude is part of daily remembrance, including in the Ardas, which gives thanks before it asks.

o: a trader who buys and sells at market
a banker or moneylender who lends capital
a king's officer who collects the taxes

games.q: the banker's capital — tap the pairs.

s: in the stanza, the banker takes back everything at once
he asks for some of it, and the man still rages.
the one who returns what's owed is made happy four times over
the stanza's reward for placing the owner's things before the owner.
the stanza promises nothing will ever be taken back
it assumes things are called back; it teaches how to hold them now.

games.q: you've lived well for years on a loan. the lender asks for part of it back. what does the wise one in the stanza do?
o: argue it's been yours too long to return.
place it back before the owner and accept the order.
hide the rest so it can't be asked for.
games.why: the wise one returns it with a bowed head, and the stanza says that one is made happy four times over.

practice: Name ten gifts you'd feel the loss of, someone's voice, your hands, a friend who still calls, a place that feels like home, and after each one, quietly add the word: lent.
Not to make you sad, only to see them as the stanza does; then close your eyes and breathe with all ten held lightly.

wordCard.voice: Saahu, a banker or moneylender: ashtpadi five's practice is gratitude, seeing what we have as the banker's capital, lent and not owned.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: saahu, a banker or moneylender; in the stanza, the One who lends us all we have.

carryVoice: Your line: count the ten. A loan, held with open hands. Four hundred fifty-seven, and counting.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
